en: The Sūtra on the Proportions for the Construction of Buddha Images, spoken by the Buddha.
Translated by Gongbu Chabu, Chief of the Tibetan Studies Bureau and Court Gentleman (Yinbin),
who served as a translator for the Manchu and Mongolian texts of the Grand Secretariat of the Qing Dynasty.

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park, together with a great assembly of bodhisattvas, śrāvaka disciples, and an immeasurable multitude of followers including humans, devas, nāgas, and spirits.
It was precisely when the World-Honored One, having preached the Dharma for his mother, was about to ascend to the realm of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra...
Ānanda paid homage to the Buddha and spoke these words: "World-Honored One, you do not abide in this world.
If there are virtuous people who cannot overcome their longing and yearn to behold the World-Honored One, and wish to create an image of your likeness, what is the proper method for doing so?"
The Buddha said, "Excellent, Śāriputra! Now I shall ascend briefly to the celestial realms.

Before I have returned from this interval, or even after I have manifested parinirvāṇa without remainder, if there are virtuous persons who wish to behold and gaze upon me, or who wish to create images for the sake of serving as a field of merit for the benefit of themselves and others, they must fashion them according to the rules of measurement for the body of the Tathāgata."
In measurement, its length and breadth are proportionate, like a nyagrodha tree, filling the full span of one fathom.
Now, regarding the dimensions of its body, limbs, and various joints, both vertical and horizontal, I shall briefly explain them to you, beginning from the uṣṇīṣa on the crown of the head.
Listen attentively and reflect well upon this. Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses:
Measured by his own fingers, he has one hundred and twenty finger-breadths. The uṣṇīṣa on his crown is four finger-breadths high; the hairline is likewise.
The vertical measurement of the face, including half of the twelve finger-breadths [of the neck], is divided into three parts: the forehead, the nose, and the chin each receive one part.
The lower portion measures four and a half finger-widths; the jaw-body is only two finger-widths. Its breadth extends toward sixteen units, and its depth is four finger-widths in diameter.
The upper lip is two finger-widths long and half that in width. In the center, it displays the shape of a *bimba* fruit, with each corner measuring one finger-width.
The length of the mouth is four finger-widths; this the wise should know. The number of teeth is forty, firm, dense, white, pure, and even.
The lower lip is six units long, and its width and depth are likewise. The groove between the lips is one-third of a finger-width in breadth.
The width of the nose measures two fingers; its height corresponds to half a finger. The nostrils are round and well-concealed; their openings are half a finger wide.
The two wings are even and perfectly circular; the nasal column spans half a finger across. The space between the eyes is eight units wide; its length should be four fingers.
The white and black portions of the iris each occupy three parts, measuring a full finger-width in extent. The black pupil is divided into five parts, with the center being the iris itself.

The width of the eye is but one foot-measure, while its protective membrane (pakṣman) is three fingers wide, shaped like the petals of a lotus flower, clear and translucent with the color of refined gold.
The *ūrṇā-kośa* (white tuft) at the *bhrū-madhya* (forehead) is broad by half a finger-width; the eyebrows are like a crescent moon, high in the center and four fingers long.

The ears are two fingers wide, their tips level with the midpoint of the eyebrows. They are transparently clear and four *pāda* (quarters) wide, with the auditory openings measuring half a finger-width.
The height of the ear is four barleycorns; its width across should be the span of a finger. The upper and lower portions within the ear are slightly less than one-fourth of a finger.
Including the hollow of the ear, the total depth is two fingers plus half a finger. The ear-flap is four and a half fingers, and the lobe of the ear is five fingers long.
The contours of his hairline are lovely beyond compare; the circumference of his head is three times that of his face, like a precious parasol, pleasing to the mind.
The distance between his two ears across the face is eighteen finger-breadths (vitasti), and the distance from behind those ears to the back of the head is fourteen finger-breadths.
The circumference of the neck is thirty-six finger-widths; the width of the vase-like neck is eight finger-widths, and its circumference is twenty-four finger-widths.

From the edge of the neck to the shoulder blade, measured horizontally, it is twelve finger-widths. The total length of the hands is four spans (vitasti), and the length of the upper arms is twenty finger-widths.
The arms have sixteen fingers; their girth is likewise. The shoulders are pointed, round, and full; their circumference at the base is twenty-four [finger-widths].
From the middle finger to the tip of the hand is exactly one span (*vitasti*). The length of the palm should be seven fingers, and its width five fingers.
The palms are flat, full, and moist, smooth and crimson, displaying all auspicious marks, adorned with spirals, wheels, flowers, and hooks.
Measuring the length of the fingers, there are five finger-widths on the front; from the middle joint of the tip of this [fore]finger to the tip of the index finger [is one such unit].
The length of the fingers when bent is less than half a finger-width compared to when straight. The tip of the little finger is pointed;
reaching the end of the bent joint, all four fingers possess three joints, with the nail-plate occupying half a joint. The thumb is four finger-widths long, and its circumference is likewise.
This refers to only two joints; the fingernail covers [the joint] as previously described. From the base of the thumb to the base of the index finger, the distance should be three fingers.

From below the base of the little finger, four and a half fingers reach the foundation. Between the nape of the neck, the heart, the navel, and the breasts, the girdle measures twelve and a half fingers.
From the tips of the breasts to the armpits, the measurement is six finger-widths. The distance between the two armpits is twenty-five finger-widths.
The circumference of the chest is exactly fifty-six finger-widths. From the two breasts down to the navel, it measures sixteen finger-widths.
The navel is circular with concentric folds; its depth and width are both one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*). The circumference of the waist at this point is forty-eight fingers.
Measured inward from the edge of the hip joints, it is twenty-four fingers. From the navel to the private organ, it measures a full span (*vitasti*) plus half a finger.
The male organ is concealed like that of a horse-king; the scrotum measures four finger-widths. The thighs are thirty-two finger-widths in girth;

their length is twenty-five finger-widths. The circumference around the knees is twenty-eight finger-widths. Including the joints, the knees measure four finger-widths; the ankle bones are three finger-widths in height.
The deer-like calves are slender, rounded, and straight; they are twenty-five finger-widths in length. Their circumference at the midpoint is twenty-one finger-widths.

The circumference of the ankles is fourteen finger-widths, with a width of two finger-widths at their sides. Below this, the heels measure four finger-widths, and their convex breadth is three finger-widths.
The sole of the foot is one span (vitasti) in length; its thickness is two finger-breadths (aṅgula). Each of the four fingers has three joints, and the nail covers half of the final joint.
The thumb has only two joints. The circumference of the five fingers is such that their total length is three finger-breadths; the index finger is likewise.
The sixteenth [mark] consists of eight parts: the middle and little fingers are bent inward; the thumb has a thickness of six *pāda*s; the remaining fingers gradually taper to full length;
the bases of the fingers are connected by a webbed membrane; the insteps are as high as a tortoise shell; the palms are flat, full, soft, and supple; and their color is glossy and deep red.
The wheel, the conch, and the auspicious letter—these wondrous marks are profound and subtle. Such are the marks of the Tathāgata, complete with all merits.
When the Buddha had finished preaching this sutra, the venerable Śāriputra, his disciples, and the entire great assembly, having heard what the Buddha taught, were all greatly rejoiced;
they believed, accepted, and practiced it accordingly.
The Sūtra on the Proportions for the Construction of Buddha Images Spoken by the Buddha.
